groups.high: Maternity benefit under the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 must be interpreted using the applicable amended version, rather than an invented twelve-week scheme. Section 46 links eligibility to at least six months' employment immediately before delivery. The restriction concerns having two or more living children at delivery, not simply having given birth twice; the provision preserves other leave to which the woman is entitled. The official consolidated text now provides sixty days before the expected delivery and sixty days after delivery. Older versions provided eight weeks on either side, so sixteen weeks and the current 120-day provision should not be conflated. Section 47 governs notice, evidence of birth, absence, and alternative payment arrangements. A woman who did not give advance notice can notify the employer within seven days after delivery; payment options and evidence requirements must be followed rather than assuming one payment date for every case. Section 48 in the consolidated text calculates average daily wages by dividing the woman's last fixed monthly total wages by twenty-six. It permits payment in cash, to a bank account, or by electronic funds transfer. This is not an eighty-four-day earnings average including every bonus or an independently established minimum-wage substitution rule. Check statutory coverage, service records, living-child condition, applicable version, wage calculation, and notice documents. The benefit is an employer payment obligation, not a description of wholly unpaid leave.
groups.mid: Maternity benefit is money paid by an employer around childbirth. Bangladesh's Labour Act, 2006 has been amended, so the version matters. Section 46 requires at least six months of work for the employer immediately before delivery. The child limit concerns two or more living children at delivery. It is not simply a count of past births. Other leave you are entitled to is still preserved. The official consolidated text now gives sixty days before the expected birth and sixty days after delivery. Older versions gave eight weeks before and eight weeks after. Do not confuse that older sixteen-week rule with the current 120 days. Section 47 covers notice, proof of birth, time away, and payment options. If you gave no advance notice, you can notify the employer within seven days after delivery. The payment and evidence rules still matter. There is not one payment date for every case. Section 48 in the consolidated text gives a daily wage calculation. Divide the woman's last fixed monthly total wages by twenty-six. Payment can be in cash, a bank account, or electronic funds transfer. It is not based on eighty-four days of earnings or every bonus. Nor does this text establish the claimed minimum-wage substitution rule. Check coverage, work records, the living-child rule, the legal version, pay, and notice papers. This benefit is the employer's duty to pay, not wholly unpaid leave.
groups.low: Maternity benefit is pay from your employer around childbirth. The Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 has changed over time. Check which version applies. Section 46 requires at least six months of work for that employer just before delivery. The child rule concerns two or more living children when you give birth. It is not just a count of past births. You can still get other leave you are entitled to. The official consolidated text now gives sixty days before the expected birth. It gives sixty days after delivery too. Older versions gave eight weeks before and eight weeks after. That was sixteen weeks, not the current 120 days. Section 47 covers notice, proof of birth, time off, and ways to pay. If you gave no advance notice, you can tell the employer within seven days after delivery. Check the proof and payment rules. Not every case has the same payment date. Section 48 gives a daily pay rule in the consolidated text. Take the woman's last fixed monthly total wages. Divide by twenty-six. Pay can be in cash, a bank account, or electronic funds transfer. It is not an eighty-four-day earnings average that adds every bonus. The text does not establish the claimed minimum-wage substitution rule either. Check who the Act covers, your work records, the living-child rule, the version, pay, and notice papers. This is a duty for the employer to pay. It is not wholly unpaid leave.

groups.notes: Corrected twelve-week/84-day benefit, wage formula, living-child condition and unpaid-leave claims; current versus historical versions explicit.

groups.high: For an adult worker covered by the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, Section 100 provides the ordinary daily working limit of eight hours, with work up to ten hours subject to Section 108's overtime provisions. The reference is Section 100, not Section 34. The eight-hour ordinary limit should not be described as including an absolute ban on all overtime, while the two additional hours do not create an unrestricted employer entitlement to compel work. Section 102 supplies the weekly framework: ordinarily forty-eight hours, up to sixty hours subject to the statutory conditions, and an annual weekly average not exceeding fifty-six hours. These limits operate together; meeting the daily ceiling alone does not establish weekly compliance. Section 101 addresses rest or meal intervals, and actual working time should be distinguished from the entire spread of attendance. Section 108 requires the applicable overtime premium rather than treating additional hours as ordinary unpaid work. Special rules, lawful exemptions, and the worker's statutory category may affect an individual case, so an unqualified assertion that every imaginable departure is illegal is too broad. Maintain actual start, finish, break, and overtime records, check both daily and weekly totals, and compare the overtime payment with the governing wage components. A contractual clause or time sheet does not itself displace statutory protections, and a breach does not establish an automatic maximum criminal penalty or liability for every later injury without the relevant legal conditions.
groups.mid: For an adult worker covered by the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, Section 100 sets the daily rule. Ordinary work is limited to eight hours. Work can extend to ten hours under the overtime rules in Section 108. The section is not Section 34. Eight hours is the ordinary limit, not a ban on every extra hour. Nor do two extra hours give an employer a free right to demand work. Section 102 gives weekly limits. Ordinary work is forty-eight hours a week. Work may reach sixty hours under the legal conditions. The weekly average over the year must not exceed fifty-six hours. Check daily and weekly totals together. Staying under ten hours a day does not prove the week is lawful. Section 101 deals with rest or meal breaks. Time spent working is not always the same as the whole time from arrival to leaving. Section 108 requires the relevant overtime pay. Extra hours are not ordinary unpaid work. Special rules, lawful exemptions, and the worker's category may matter. Keep real start, finish, break, and overtime records. Check pay against the wage components the law uses. A contract or time sheet does not replace legal rights. A breach does not automatically mean the maximum penalty or liability for every later injury.
groups.low: Section 100 gives the daily rule in the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006. It covers adult workers within the Act. Ordinary work is limited to eight hours a day. Work can reach ten hours under the overtime rules in Section 108. This is not Section 34. Eight hours does not ban every extra hour. But the extra two hours are not a free right for a boss to demand work. Section 102 gives weekly rules. Ordinary work is forty-eight hours a week. Work may reach sixty hours under the legal conditions. The weekly average over a year must not exceed fifty-six hours. Check both the day and the week. Ten hours or less each day does not prove the week meets the rules. Section 101 covers rest or meal breaks. Time at work is not always all time spent working. Section 108 requires the relevant overtime pay. Extra hours are not ordinary unpaid work. Special rules, lawful exemptions, and the kind of worker may matter. Keep the real times you start, finish, take breaks, and work overtime. Check the pay and the wage parts used to work it out. A contract or time sheet does not replace legal rights. A breach does not always mean the maximum penalty. It does not by itself prove liability for every later injury.

groups.high: Section 26 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 governs employer termination otherwise than through the other specified modes, rather than Sections 35–37. For a permanent worker, it requires written notice of 120 days if employed on monthly wages, or sixty days for other permanent workers. Other permanent workers must not be equated with every casual, temporary, or daily-paid person. Section 26 separately provides thirty days for monthly-rated temporary workers and fourteen days for other temporary workers, subject to the specified exception for completion, cessation, abolition, or abandonment of the temporary work. The employer may pay wages in lieu of the required notice; accordingly, immediate departure with lawful payment is not necessarily summary dismissal or wrongful termination. For permanent workers, Section 26 also provides compensation for completed years of service or gratuity if payable, whichever is higher, in addition to other benefits due; apply the operative text and wage definition rather than inventing damages for mental anguish. Retrenchment, discharge, dismissal for misconduct, resignation, and termination with notice have distinct statutory conditions. Misconduct proceedings engage their own safeguards and should not be relabeled as ordinary termination to bypass them. Identify worker classification, wage basis, termination route, written notice or payment, service duration, and outstanding benefits. Preserve appointment documents, wage records, notice, and proof of receipt, and obtain timely advice about the applicable grievance route rather than assuming reinstatement or additional damages are automatic.
groups.mid: Section 26 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 covers this kind of employer termination. Termination means ending the job. The rule is not in Sections 35–37. A permanent worker paid monthly must get written notice. The period is 120 days. Other permanent workers must get sixty days. Other permanent workers does not mean every casual or temporary worker. Section 26 has separate rules for temporary workers. Notice is thirty days for those paid monthly and fourteen days for others. An exception concerns the temporary work being completed, stopped, abolished, or abandoned. The employer can pay wages instead of the required notice. So leaving at once with lawful payment is not always wrongful termination or dismissal for misconduct. Permanent workers also have a Section 26 right to compensation for completed years of service or gratuity if payable, whichever is higher. Other benefits due are separate. Check the operative text and wage rule. Do not assume extra damages for distress. Retrenchment and discharge have their own rules. So do misconduct dismissal and resignation. Termination with notice is a separate route. Misconduct proceedings have their own safeguards. A different label should not be used to avoid them. Check your worker category, wage basis, reason for the legal route, notice or pay, service length, and benefits owed. Keep appointment papers, wage records, the notice, and proof of receipt. Seek timely advice about the grievance route. Reinstatement and extra damages are not automatic.
groups.low: Section 26 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 covers this way a boss ends a job. It is not Sections 35–37. A permanent worker paid monthly must get 120 days of written notice. Other permanent workers must get sixty days. That does not mean every casual or temporary worker gets sixty days. Temporary workers have separate rules. They get thirty days if paid monthly and fourteen days if paid another way. An exception concerns temporary work that is completed, stopped, abolished, or abandoned. A boss can pay wages instead of giving the required notice. So ending work at once with lawful pay is not always wrongful termination or misconduct dismissal. Section 26 also gives permanent workers a right to compensation. This is pay for completed years of service. Gratuity may be due instead. It is another kind of leaving payment. Use the higher amount. Other benefits are separate. They are still owed. Check the text in force and the wage rule. Do not assume extra pay for distress. Retrenchment has its own rules. So does discharge. A misconduct dismissal is different too. Resignation means you choose to leave. Termination with notice is a separate route. Misconduct proceedings have safeguards. A boss should not use another label to avoid them. Check your worker type and pay basis. Check which legal route is used. Check notice or pay. Check how long you worked. Check the benefits owed. Keep appointment papers, pay records, the notice, and proof you got it. Ask for timely advice about a grievance. Getting the job back or extra damages is not automatic.
groups.source_review: Official consolidated Section26 checked, including permanent/temporary distinction and payment in lieu; no fabricated case law used.
groups.notes: Corrected section references, classification, oral-notice implication, immediate-termination prohibition and unsupported damages.

groups.high: Chapter XII of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 establishes compensation for specified employment injuries. Section 150, not Section 43, links employer liability to personal injury caused by an accident arising out of and in the course of employment. Specified occupational diseases can be treated as employment injuries under the statutory conditions; this does not automatically include every stress disorder or illness occurring during working hours. The provision contains exclusions. These include incapacity not exceeding three days, and specified nonfatal injuries directly attributable to intoxication, wilful disobedience of an express safety order or rule, or wilful removal or disregard of a known safety device. The fatal versus nonfatal qualification matters; ordinary carelessness is not automatically the same as those exclusions. Section 151 and the relevant schedules determine compensation by the applicable injury category, including death, permanent total or partial disablement, and temporary disablement. It is not a universal age-based common-law damages formula or a guarantee of every claimed expense. Section 157 generally requires notice as soon as practicable and a claim within two years of the accident or death, while statutory exceptions can preserve claims with notice defects or sufficient cause. Medical assessment and employment evidence matter. Preserve the incident account, witness information, treatment records, wages, and employment documents; obtain prompt assistance from the appropriate labour authority or legal adviser. Do not confuse accident reporting, medical examination, a compensation claim, and an appeal as one universal thirty-day process.
groups.mid: The Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 has a work-injury rule. It is in Chapter XII. Compensation means money paid for the harm. Section 150 is the key rule, not Section 43. An accident must cause a personal injury arising out of and in the course of employment. This means the job link matters. Specified work diseases can count under the legal conditions. Not every illness or stress problem at work automatically counts. There are exclusions. One is incapacity lasting no more than three days. Some nonfatal injuries are excluded too. Nonfatal means the worker did not die. The direct cause must fit the rule. It may be intoxication, meaning the effects of drink or drugs. It may be wilfully breaking a clear safety rule or order. It may be wilfully removing or ignoring a known safety device. The nonfatal condition matters. Ordinary carelessness is not always the same thing. Section 151 and the relevant schedules set compensation. Categories include death. They include permanent total or partial disablement. They include temporary disablement too. These mean different forms of lost ability to work. There is no one age-based damages formula or promise to pay every expense claimed. Section 157 generally requires notice as soon as practicable. The claim is generally due within two years of the accident or death. Legal exceptions may allow notice defects or sufficient cause. Medical findings and proof of employment matter. Keep the incident account, witness details, treatment records, wages, and work papers. Get prompt help from the relevant labour authority or legal adviser. Accident reporting, medical checks, claims, and appeals are not one thirty-day process.
groups.low: The Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 has work-injury rules in Chapter XII. Section 150 is the key rule. It is not Section 43. An accident must cause the injury. It must arise out of and in the course of the job. The job link matters. Some work diseases can count under the rules. Not every illness or stress problem at work counts. There are exclusions. One is being unable to work fully or partly for no more than three days. Some nonfatal injuries are excluded too. The direct cause must fit the rule. This can be intoxication. This means the effects of drink or drugs. It can be wilfully breaking a clear safety rule or order. It can be wilfully removing a known safety device. Wilfully ignoring one can count too. Nonfatal means the worker did not die. Ordinary carelessness is not always the same thing. Section 151 and the relevant schedules set the amounts. They cover death and loss of ability to work. That loss may be permanent or temporary, and total or partial. There is no one damages formula based on age. Not every claimed expense is promised. Section 157 generally says to give notice as soon as practicable. A claim is generally due within two years. This runs from the accident or death. Legal exceptions may apply. These may allow a fault in the notice or a good reason for delay. Keep notes on what happened. Keep witness names. Keep medical records, pay records, and work papers. Get help promptly. Ask the relevant labour authority or legal adviser. Reporting is one step. Medical checks are another. Claims and appeals have their own rules. These are not one thirty-day process.
groups.source_review: Official ChapterXII Sections150,151,157 checked, including explicit exclusions and exceptions; no invented judicial presumptions retained.
groups.notes: Corrected section43, blanket coverage, age/wage formula, burden-shift and30-day claims.

groups.high: Overtime entitlement under Section 108 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 is calculated at twice the ordinary rate of basic wages, dearness allowance, and ad hoc or interim pay, if any, for work beyond the prescribed daily or weekly hours. The relevant section is 108, not 35. Dearness allowance is the specified cost-of-living component; ad hoc or interim pay should not be redefined as every regular allowance. The statutory components are therefore not automatically synonymous with total gross salary. Housing, transport, bonuses, incentives, or other payments should not be added merely because they appear on a pay slip; determine whether a component falls within the applicable legal basis. If the correctly derived ordinary hourly rate of the covered components is BDT 100, the overtime rate is BDT 200 per hour, so three qualifying hours yield BDT 600. Multiplying a monthly sum by two does not by itself produce an hourly rate, and dividing by twenty-six without the relevant hours conversion does not complete that calculation. Applicable rules, worker classification, and any special treatment of piece-rate work must also be checked. Record actual qualifying hours, the component amounts, the conversion method, and payments made. Overtime pay does not itself authorize excessive hours: Sections 100 and 102 impose separate daily and weekly constraints. Use the operative Act and rules rather than a contract's convenient denominator or an unsupported gross-wage formula.
groups.mid: Section 108 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 sets overtime pay. The section is not Section 35. For qualifying work beyond the daily or weekly limit, pay is twice the ordinary rate of basic wages, dearness allowance, and ad hoc or interim pay, if any. Dearness allowance is the named cost-of-living part. Ad hoc or interim pay does not mean every regular allowance. So these parts are not always the same as the whole gross salary. Do not add housing, transport, bonuses, or incentives just because they appear on a pay slip. Check which parts the law covers. Suppose the correct ordinary hourly rate for those parts is BDT 100. The overtime rate is BDT 200 an hour. Three qualifying overtime hours then give BDT 600. Doubling a monthly amount does not turn it into an hourly rate. Dividing by twenty-six alone does not finish the hourly calculation either. The relevant hours conversion is still needed. Check the rules, worker type, and any special treatment of piece-rate work. Piece rate means pay for units of work. Keep actual hours, wage parts, the conversion method, and payments. Paying overtime does not permit too many hours. Sections 100 and 102 have separate daily and weekly limits. Use the Act and rules in force, not a convenient contract divisor or an unproved gross-pay formula.
groups.low: Section 108 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 sets overtime pay. It is not Section 35. Qualifying extra work beyond the daily or weekly limit is paid at twice the ordinary rate. The covered parts are basic wages, dearness allowance, and ad hoc or interim pay, if any. Dearness allowance is the named cost-of-living part. Ad hoc or interim pay does not mean every regular allowance. The covered parts are not always the whole gross salary. Do not add housing, transport, bonuses, or incentives just because they are on a pay slip. Check which parts the law covers. Say the correct ordinary hourly rate for those parts is BDT 100. The overtime rate is BDT 200 an hour. Three qualifying extra hours give BDT 600. Doubling a monthly sum does not make an hourly rate. Dividing by twenty-six alone does not finish it either. You still need the relevant hours conversion. Check the rules, worker type, and any special treatment of piece-rate work. Piece rate means pay for units of work. Keep the real hours, wage parts, method of conversion, and payments. Overtime pay does not allow too many hours. Sections 100 and 102 set separate daily and weekly limits. Use the Act and rules in force. Do not rely on a convenient contract divisor or an unproved gross-pay formula.

groups.high: ILO Convention No. 155, the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981, protects withdrawal from serious imminent danger through Article 13, not Article 15. A worker who has reasonable justification to believe a work situation presents imminent and serious danger to life or health is to be protected from undue consequences after removing themselves, in accordance with national conditions and practice. The reasonable-belief qualification matters; the Convention does not require a worker to wait for an injury, but neither does it create an unconditional right to terminate employment on any asserted concern. Article 19(f) complements this protection by requiring arrangements for prompt reporting to the immediate supervisor and preventing an employer from requiring return while the imminent and serious danger continues, until necessary remedial action has been taken. Dismissal, punitive demotion, threats, or other adverse treatment may raise protection concerns, but the Convention alone does not prescribe an automatic reversal of the burden of proof or a universal damages award. Domestic implementation determines the forum, procedures, remedies, and the precise operation of the protection. Move to safety, report the hazard promptly when safe, document the facts supporting the reasonable belief, and seek the relevant safety representative or authority. An illustrative hazard such as exposed live machinery requires an assessment of actual conditions, not a guarantee that every discomfort constitutes the Convention's threshold. Protecting life and health and making the danger safe are the central objectives.
groups.mid: ILO Convention No. 155 is the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981. Article 13 protects a worker who leaves a work situation. They must reasonably believe it presents imminent and serious danger to life or health. Imminent means the danger is about to happen or is close. The worker should be protected from undue consequences under national conditions and practice. The rule is not Article 15. A worker does not have to wait to be hurt. But a reasonable belief matters. This is not an unconditional right to end a job for any concern. Article 19(f) adds a reporting and return rule. Workers must be able to report such danger promptly. They report to the immediate supervisor. Needed action must make it safe. An employer cannot require return while the imminent and serious danger continues. Dismissal can raise protection concerns. So can a punitive demotion or threats. A punitive demotion means a lower rank used as punishment. It does not alone set who must prove a case everywhere. It does not promise one damages award. Domestic law sets the forum, process, and remedies. Move to safety. Report promptly when safe. Keep notes on the facts. Explain why you reasonably thought the danger was serious and imminent. Seek help. Ask a safety representative or relevant authority. Exposed live machinery may be a serious hazard. The actual conditions matter. Not every discomfort meets the test. The aim is to protect life and health and make the danger safe.
groups.low: ILO Convention No. 155 is the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981. Article 13 protects a worker who leaves a dangerous work situation. The worker must have reasonable grounds to believe it puts life or health in imminent and serious danger. Imminent means close or about to happen. The worker should be protected from undue consequences. National conditions and practice matter. The rule is not Article 15. You do not have to wait to get hurt. But the belief must be reasonable. This is not a free right to end a job for any concern. Article 19(f) adds rules. Workers must be able to report such danger promptly to the immediate supervisor. A boss cannot require a return while the imminent and serious danger continues. Needed action must first deal with it. Dismissal, a punitive demotion, or threats may raise protection concerns. The Convention does not by itself shift the burden of proof in every case. It does not promise one damages award everywhere. Domestic law sets the forum, process, and remedies. Move to safety. Report promptly when safe. Keep facts that show why you reasonably thought the danger was serious and imminent. Ask a safety representative or relevant authority for help. Exposed live machinery may be a serious hazard. The actual facts matter. Not every discomfort meets the test. The aim is to protect life and health and make the danger safe.

groups.notes: Corrected Article15 and absolute termination/burden-shift claims. National conditions and reasonable justification preserved.

groups.high: Article 16 of ILO Convention No. 155, the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981, sets the relevant employer responsibilities, not Article 5. Employers are to be required to ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, that workplaces, machinery, equipment, and processes under their control are safe and without risk to health. Article 16 also addresses chemical, physical, and biological substances and agents under employer control, with appropriate protective measures, and necessary protective clothing and equipment to prevent accidents or adverse health effects. The reasonably-practicable qualification and scope of control must not be replaced with an absolute promise of zero risk. Article 19 provides for worker cooperation, information, consultation, and appropriate safety training; Article 17 concerns cooperation where undertakings operate simultaneously at one workplace. In practical implementation, assessment of hazards, effective guarding, suitable maintenance, safe operating procedures, and training can support the duty. These are examples of prevention, not a fixed inspection interval stated by Article 16. Protective equipment should be appropriate to the hazard rather than used as a substitute for making dangerous machinery safe. Domestic law and implementation determine inspection powers, offences, compensation, and particular sanctions; the Convention itself does not automatically impose every claimed civil or criminal penalty or reverse evidentiary burdens. Check the equipment and process, who controls them, actual protective measures, worker instruction, and the applicable national rules. Records of checks, defects, repairs, and training can help demonstrate what was done.
groups.mid: ILO Convention No. 155 is the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981. Article 16 gives the relevant employer duties, not Article 5. Employers must be required to make things under their control safe and without risk to health. This covers workplaces, machinery, equipment, and processes. The standard is so far as reasonably practicable. This is not an absolute promise of zero risk. What is under the employer's control matters too. Article 16 also covers substances and agents. These may be chemical, physical, or biological. It requires appropriate protective measures. Necessary protective clothing and equipment help prevent accidents or harm to health. Article 19 covers worker cooperation and information. It includes consultation and suitable safety training. Article 17 concerns firms working at the same workplace. In practice, a firm can assess hazards. It can fit effective guards. It can maintain equipment and use safe work procedures. It can train workers. These are examples of prevention. Article 16 does not set one inspection interval for every machine. Protective equipment must fit the hazard. It should not replace making a dangerous machine safe. Domestic law sets inspection powers and offences. It sets compensation and sanctions too. Sanctions are penalties. The Convention does not impose every claimed civil or criminal penalty on its own. It does not automatically change who must prove a case. Check the equipment and process. Check who controls them. Check protective measures, instructions, and national rules. Keep records of checks, faults, repairs, and training to show what was done.
groups.low: ILO Convention No. 155 is the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981. Article 16 gives the relevant employer duties. It is not Article 5. Employers must be required to make things they control safe. These include the workplace, machines, and equipment. They include processes: how work is done. They must be without risk to health, so far as reasonably practicable. This means taking feasible steps in light of the risk. It is not a promise of zero risk. What the employer controls matters too. Article 16 covers substances and agents. They may be chemical, physical, or biological. These are different things that can harm health. The right steps to protect health are needed. Needed protective clothing and equipment must be provided. They help prevent accidents and harm to health. Article 19 covers how workers and bosses cooperate. They work together on safety. It covers information: facts workers need. It covers consultation: asking for views. It covers suitable safety training too. Workers need to know the risks and how to work safely. Article 17 concerns firms working at the same site. A firm can check hazards and fit effective guards. It can keep machines in good order. It can set safe work steps and train workers. These are ways to prevent harm. Article 16 does not set one check interval for all machines. Protective equipment must fit the hazard. For example, a guard can keep a hand from moving parts. Gloves alone may not make a machine safe. Needed protection should not replace making a dangerous machine safe. Domestic law sets who can inspect a site and what they can do. It sets offences, compensation, and sanctions. These mean acts against the law, pay for harm, and penalties. The treaty does not impose every claimed civil or criminal penalty on its own. It does not automatically change who must prove a case. Check the equipment and process. Check who controls them. Check how people are protected. Check instructions and national rules. A loose guard or a fault needs a safe fix, not just a note in a book. Keep records of checks and faults. Keep records of repairs and training.

groups.notes: Corrected Article5, zero-risk absolute mandate, and universal liability/burden claims.

groups.high: Article 21 of ILO Convention No. 155, the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981, states the principle that occupational safety and health measures should not involve expenditure for workers. The relevant provision is Article 21, not Article 4, which concerns national policy. The principle addresses financing safety measures, including necessary protective equipment; a compulsory purchase or wage deduction that transfers the expense of an employer's required safety measure to a worker is inconsistent with that allocation. Article 16 supplies related employer responsibilities for safe workplaces, machinery, processes, substances, and necessary protective clothing and equipment, while Article 19 addresses cooperation, information, and appropriate training. Maintenance and proper use of necessary protective equipment are not a reason to shift its safety-related expense onto workers. However, the Convention should not be paraphrased as automatically invalidating every union due, every insurance premium, or every deduction regardless of purpose and domestic law. The actual charge and whether it finances a covered safety measure matter. Nor does Article 21 establish a universal guarantee that all litigation, remediation, or ordinary personal expenses have identical funding rules. National implementation supplies the specific enforcement route and remedies. Identify the required measure, who requires it, the proposed payment or deduction, and the applicable national rules; keep receipts, wage slips, and safety instructions if a charge is disputed. Prevention costs should be allocated without making workers finance the measures intended to protect them.
groups.mid: Article 21 gives the no-cost rule in ILO Convention No. 155. Occupational safety and health measures must not cost workers money. The full name is the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981. The rule is not Article 4. Article 4 concerns national policy. A worker should not fund a required safety measure. This includes a forced purchase or money taken from wages. Necessary protective equipment is an important example. Article 16 gives related duties for workplaces and machinery. It covers processes and substances. It covers needed protective clothing and equipment too. Article 19 concerns cooperation and information. It includes suitable training. Maintaining and properly using necessary protective equipment is also a safety measure. That is not a reason to pass its safety cost to workers. Article 21 does not make every charge invalid. This includes union dues, insurance premiums, and wage deductions. Check what each charge is for. Check what the charge pays for. Check whether it funds a covered safety measure. Domestic law matters too. Not every expense has the same funding rule. A court case may differ. So may repair after harm or an ordinary personal expense. National rules set how to enforce the rule. They set what remedy is available. Ask what measure is required. Ask who requires it. Ask who must pay. Check the national rules. Keep receipts, pay slips, and safety instructions if you dispute a charge. Workers should not have to fund the safety measures meant to protect them.
groups.low: ILO Convention No. 155 has a rule in Article 21. Safety and health measures must not cost workers money. Its full name is the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981. This rule is not Article 4. That article concerns national policy. A worker should not have to buy a required safety measure. They should not pay for it through a wage deduction either. Necessary protective equipment is an example. Article 16 gives related employer duties. It covers workplaces and machinery. It covers processes and substances. It covers needed protective clothing and equipment too. Article 19 concerns cooperation and information. It includes suitable training. Necessary protective equipment must be kept in good order. It must be used properly. These are safety measures too. That is not a reason to pass the safety cost to workers. But Article 21 does not make every charge invalid. This includes union dues. It includes insurance premiums and wage deductions. The purpose of the charge matters. Check what the charge pays for. Check if it funds a covered safety measure. Domestic law matters. Not every cost has the same rule. Court costs may differ. So may steps to repair harm or ordinary personal costs. National rules set how to enforce the rule. They set what remedy is available. Ask what measure is required. Ask who requires it. Ask who is being made to pay. Check the national rules. Keep receipts, pay slips, and safety instructions if you dispute a charge.
